Panama came to the young United Nations with a draft Declaration on the Rights and Duties of States. It was a bid to write down the basic rules of how states must treat each other. Resolution 38, passed on 11 December 1946, sets the draft on a long road of review. The Secretary-General must send the text at once to all member states and to bodies that work on world law.

Comments were due back by 1 June 1947. The draft then goes to a new Assembly team charged with the study of how world law should be codified. That team must report to the second regular session, and the question earns a place on that session's agenda.

Trust between states can be built in space as on earth, argues Resolution A/69/38, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The vote recalls a chain of texts since 2005 on trust-building steps in outer space. It also recalls a 1993 report of the Secretary-General, which held a study by state experts on how such steps could work above the earth.

All states hold the right to study and use space under world law, the text affirms. To bar an arms race in space serves peace for all, and it is a must for joint work in the peaceful use of space. Open word on space plans, shared by all, is the path the vote commends.

Resolution 138, adopted on 23 June 1960, examines Argentina's complaint about Adolf Eichmann. Israeli agents had seized Eichmann, a former Nazi officer accused of mass crimes against the Jews, and taken him from Argentina to Israel to stand trial. Argentina said the transfer violated its sovereignty.

The Council agrees that violating a member state's sovereignty clashes with the Charter, and warns that repeats of such acts would breed insecurity and distrust. At the same time, it notes the worldwide condemnation of Nazi persecution and the wish that Eichmann face proper justice. It states plainly that the resolution must not be read as excusing the crimes he was accused of.

Rafal Farjo, Jeff Skaggs, Alexander Quiambao, and co-authors delivered genes to the eye without using a virus in work published in 2006. Gene therapy for eye disease often rides on viruses, which carry risks. The alternative tested here was compacted DNA nanoparticles: the therapeutic DNA squeezed into tiny particles that cells can absorb.

The team reported efficient non-viral transfer into eye tissue. Efficiency is the hurdle for nanoparticle methods, so clearing it in the eye, an accessible and well-contained organ, was a meaningful step. Success there points toward repeatable, safer gene treatments for inherited blindness and other eye disorders, where a viral carrier's one-shot limits are a real problem.
un-sc-res-738:
Security Council Resolution 738, adopted on January 29, 1992, recommended Tajikistan for membership in the United Nations. Tajikistan had declared independence from the Soviet Union in September 1991, weeks before the union itself came apart. The poorest of the new central Asian republics, it moved at once to claim a place in the world body.

The Assembly admitted Tajikistan on March 2, in the same wave as its neighbors. Together, the authors report, the two signals switch on the ERK pathway and produce synaptic depression, a lasting weakening of connections between neurons. That weakening is one way the brain stores and updates information. The paper helps explain how reward-related dopamine and memory circuits interact at the molecular level.
plos-pone-0000238:
Hyemyung Seo, Kai-Christian Sonntag, Woori Kim, and colleagues published this Huntington's disease study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Huntington's is caused by a faulty protein that builds up in brain cells. The authors test a proteasome activator, a compound that boosts the cell's protein-shredding machinery, in neuronal model cells of the disease.

The title reports enhanced survival of the model cells with the activator. Helping cells clear toxic protein is one of the main strategies against Huntington's and similar diseases. The study gives that strategy a concrete test, showing boosted cleanup can keep sick neurons alive longer in the dish.
plos-pone-0000338:
David M. Gamm, Shaomei Wang, Bin Lu, and colleagues published this eye therapy study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Human neural progenitors are immature cells that can support or replace retinal cells. In a rat model of retinal disease, the authors report that these progenitors protect visual functions, preserving sight in the treated animals.

Cell treatments that protect rather than rebuild are nearer to clinical use. The authors measure preserved vision in the model, not just surviving cells. The study supports developing progenitor transplants for retinal diseases that currently end in blindness.
plos-pone-0000438:
Ripan S. Malhi and colleagues built a genetics resource for the rhesus macaque, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Macaques are among the most used animals in medical research because their biology closely matches ours. The team catalogued SNPs, single-letter DNA differences, in Macaca mulatta, giving the resource the name Mamu SNP.

A shared catalogue of genetic differences lets researchers compare animals properly, check breeding colonies, and link genes to traits and diseases. Without it, each lab rediscovers the same variants. Resources like this rarely make headlines, but they quietly raise the quality of every primate study that uses them.
plos-pone-0000538:
Michelle L. Hastings and colleagues showed how two general splicing factors steer the editing of gene messages, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Splicing cuts introns out of pre-mRNA and joins the rest; it is controlled by factors including PUF60 and U2AF65. The team examined how these general factors control pre-mRNA splicing decisions.

General factors touch thousands of messages, so their control logic shapes the whole proteome. Mis-splicing underlies many genetic diseases and cancers. Detailing how PUF60 and U2AF65 choose splice sites gives drug developers something concrete. These choice points can, in principle, be nudged. The goal would be to correct a patient's faulty message.
plos-pone-0000638:
Jeffrey A. Johnson, Jin-Fen Li, Xierong Wei and co-authors presented simpler tests for HIV drug resistance in PLOS ONE in 2007. Antiretroviral therapy fails when HIV-1 becomes resistant to the drugs. Standard bulk sequencing finds resistance only when resistant virus is fairly common. Clinicians also needed to judge the low-frequency resistant variants hiding below that detection limit.

Their PCR assays, aimed at HIV-1 subtype B, raise the sensitivity of resistance testing. The title adds a second gain: the assays can link resistance mutations together on the same virus. Knowing which mutations travel together changes how a treatment plan reads a test result.
plos-pone-0000738:
Ann-Brit Eg Hansen, Nicolai Lohse, Jan Gerstoft and colleagues examined deaths among siblings of patients carrying both HIV and hepatitis C. Their 2007 PLOS ONE finding is stark. Co-infection is linked with three- to four-fold higher mortality among the patients' siblings. The comparison groups were siblings of HIV-only patients and population controls. Dead siblings never caught the patients' viruses, so something else must be shared.

The authors break the excess down by cause of death. Their reading is that risk factors shared by family members partly explain the pattern. Families share habits, environments, and sometimes drug use or poverty. This study turns an individual infection into a family-level warning sign.
plos-pone-0000838:
Bonnie R. Pedersen, Deborah Kamwendo, Melinda Blood and colleagues studied whether a mother's HIV-related genes affect transmission to her child, in Malawi. Variants in the CCR5 and CCR2 genes have been associated with protection against HIV transmission in adults and with delayed progression to AIDS. The CCR5 delta-32 deletion and another variant are associated with reduced expression of the CCR5 protein, the doorway HIV uses to enter cells.

The team investigated associations between CCR5 haplotypes, combinations of variants inherited together, and mother-to-child transmission. If a child's or mother's gene pattern lowers CCR5, transmission odds may fall. Such knowledge could sharpen prevention for the highest-risk pairs.
plos-pone-0000938:
Wilfried Thuiller, Jasper Slingsby, Sean Privett and colleagues studied how plant species replace each other in a fire prone region, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Cape Floristic Region of South Africa is one of the richest plant areas on Earth. Keeping so many species side by side needs explaining.

Using a long term data set, the team test whether chance turnover of species can sit alongside stable coexistence. Fire resets the stage there at intervals, and species must return or yield. Their analysis works at both local and wider scales. The results matter for managers who must keep this hotspot diverse under a changing climate.
plos-pone-0001038:
Malcolm Semple, Hinke Dankert, Bahram Ebrahimi and colleagues compared airway chemistry in infants with severe RSV illness, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Respiratory syncytial virus causes bronchiolitis, a swelling of the small airways, and some previously well infants become severely ill. Differences in the first immune response may explain why.

The team tested whether two airway factors differ with severity: interferon gamma, an antiviral signal, and substance P, a nerve related chemical. Their title reports both are reduced in severe cases. A weaker early response in the airway itself could let the virus do more damage. The measures may also help flag infants at risk.
plos-pone-0001138:
Ovarian cancer often responds well to first chemotherapy, then returns in a drug-resistant form. Marianne Tuefferd and a multicenter French group, GINECO, examined a possible drug target in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The target is HER2, a growth signal protein already used to guide treatment in breast cancer.

The study measured HER2 status in ovarian cancers from 320 patients. Targeted drugs such as trastuzumab exist for HER2-driven tumors, so knowing how often ovarian cancers carry the marker matters for trial design. The paper gives a large, multi-center count of how common HER2 positivity is in this disease.
plos-pone-0001238:

Arturo Briva and colleagues studied how high carbon dioxide levels affect the lung's lining cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Those levels build up in patients whose lungs are failing. Mechanical ventilation maintains gas exchange but can itself injure the lung.

The authors report that high CO2 levels impair alveolar epithelial function independently of pH. The harm comes from the CO2 itself, not just the acidity it creates. That distinction matters for ventilator strategies that tolerate high CO2 to protect the lung. Their result says tolerance may carry its own cost.
plos-pone-0001338:
New blood vessels in tumors grow with the help of endothelial progenitor cells from the bone marrow. Alessia Ciarrocchi and colleagues studied a regulator of those cells, Id1, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Loss of Id1 in the bone marrow severely impairs tumor angiogenesis and significantly inhibits tumor growth, a phenotype tied to missing circulating progenitor cells.

The authors report that Id1 restrains p21 expression to control endothelial progenitor cell formation. p21 is a brake on cell division; Id1 keeps it in check so progenitors can be produced. The pathway offers targets for starving tumors of their blood supply.
plos-pone-0001438:

If the world warms, disease rates may shift too. The team built a step by step model of the disease, called schistosomiasis.

Their model links heat to snail numbers, worm growth, and human cases. It then tests how control steps would fare as heat changes. Models like this help health teams plan years ahead, not just for one season. They also flag where field data are most needed to firm up forecasts.
plos-pone-0001538:

Their tree sorts the main TB lines and their order of split. Even a near uniform germ holds a readable past in rare changes. That past helps track how strains spread and gain drug resistance. It also frames why some lines thrive in set regions.
plos-pone-0001638:
Matthew G. Cottingham, Rikke F. Andersen, Alexandra J. Spencer, and their co-authors built a new genetic tool for working with a vaccine virus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Using recombination-based engineering, often called recombineering, they could add expression units or change genes in the viral genome far faster than with older methods. plos-pone-0001738:
Katsuhiko Hayashi and co-authors showed that mice need microRNA production to make germ cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. plos-pone-0001838:
Daniel J. Kliebenstein examined how gene duplication shapes plant metabolism in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Most plant and animal genomes have been through whole genome doublings during their history. Kliebenstein adds another process: natural variation of gene expression between plants and groups as a driver of how plant chemistry evolves. The full text lays out the evidence and the argument across plant pathways. Metabolism is where genes meet the environment, so how doubled copies diversify helps explain the chemistry that lets plants make medicines, poisons, and flavors.
plos-pone-0001938:

How they cross was still debated. The team tested penetratin on fluid membrane domains, the soft films that mimic a cell wall, and watched the shape of the film. They report that the peptide induces curvature in the film. A bend in the wall may be the first step by which such peptides get in.
plos-pone-0002038:

plos-pone-0002138:

plos-pone-0002238:

plos-pone-0002338:

plos-pone-0003138:

plos-pone-0003338:
